notes.definition: A system is an object or group of objects. When a system changes, energy is transferred between its stores (and to or from the surroundings), but the total amount of energy stays the same.
explanation: Physicists describe energy using stores and pathways. Energy can be held in a kinetic store (moving objects), a gravitational potential store (objects raised in a gravitational field), an elastic potential store (stretched or squashed objects), a thermal store (also called internal energy), a chemical store (fuels, food, batteries), a magnetic store, an electrostatic store or a nuclear store. Energy is not a substance: these stores are a way of keeping track of how much energy a system has and where it is.

Energy moves between stores along four pathways. It can be transferred mechanically, when a force does work (for example pushing, pulling or stretching). It can be transferred electrically, when a current flows and the charge does work. It can be transferred by heating, from a hotter object to a cooler one. It can also be transferred by radiation, such as light or sound waves carrying energy away from a source.

A system is whatever object or group of objects you choose to study. In a closed system no energy enters or leaves, so there is no net change in the total energy, even though energy moves between stores inside the system. Choosing the system carefully matters: a falling ball and the Earth together can be treated as a closed system if air resistance is ignored.

AQA expects you to describe the changes in common situations. When an object is projected upwards, its kinetic store decreases and its gravitational potential store increases. When a moving object hits an obstacle, its kinetic store decreases and energy is transferred to thermal stores (and as sound). When a constant force accelerates an object, work done by the force increases its kinetic store. When a vehicle slows down, its kinetic store decreases and the thermal stores of the brakes and surroundings increase. When water is boiled in a kettle, energy is transferred electrically to the heating element and then by heating to the thermal store of the water.

You can also use calculations to show on a common scale how the total energy is redistributed. Because energy is conserved, the decrease in one store must equal the total increase in all the other stores plus any energy dissipated to the surroundings. For example, if a toy car's chemical store falls by 450 J and its kinetic store gains 90 J while 60 J is carried away as sound, then the remaining 300 J must have gone to thermal stores.
keyFacts: A system is an object or a group of objects.
The eight energy stores are kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal (internal), chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear.
Energy is transferred mechanically (by forces doing work), electrically, by heating or by radiation.
Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed.
In a closed system there is no net change in the total energy.
When a system changes, the decrease in one store equals the total increase in the other stores (including energy dissipated).
An object projected upwards: kinetic store decreases, gravitational potential store increases.
A vehicle braking: kinetic store decreases, thermal stores of the brakes and surroundings increase.
Energy is measured in joules (J); 1 kJ = 1000 J.

keyTerms.definition: An object or group of objects being studied.
A system where no energy is transferred in or out, so the total energy in it does not change.
A way energy is held by a system, such as kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal or chemical.
The way energy is transferred between stores: mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation.
Energy transferred mechanically when a force moves an object, or electrically when a current flows.
Energy that spreads out into the surroundings, usually into thermal stores, in a way that is not useful.
The energy stored by the particles of an object; it increases when the object is heated.

workedExamples.title: Describing a system change
workedExamples.question: A student lifts a book from the floor onto a shelf. Describe the changes in the way energy is stored.
steps: Define the system: the student, the book and the Earth.
The chemical store of the student's muscles decreases.
The student does work on the book (a mechanical transfer), so the book's gravitational potential store increases.
Some energy is dissipated: the thermal stores of the student's muscles and the surroundings increase.
workedExamples.answer: Chemical store of the student decreases; energy is transferred mechanically to the gravitational potential store of the book, with some dissipated to thermal stores.

workedExamples.title: Redistribution of energy with a unit conversion
workedExamples.question: A cyclist's chemical store decreases by 1.5 kJ while she speeds up. Her kinetic store increases by 420 J. Calculate the energy dissipated to the surroundings in joules.
steps: Convert to the same unit: 1.5 kJ = 1.5 × 1000 = 1500 J.
Energy is conserved, so energy dissipated = decrease in chemical store minus increase in kinetic store.

workedExamples.title: Showing energy on a common scale
workedExamples.question: A ball has 12 J in its gravitational potential store when dropped. Just before hitting the ground its kinetic store is 11.4 J. Explain where the rest of the energy has gone and calculate it.
steps: The gravitational potential store decreases by 12 J (it reaches zero at the ground).
The kinetic store increases by 11.4 J.
This 0.6 J was transferred mechanically by work done against air resistance, increasing the thermal stores of the ball and the air.
workedExamples.answer: 0.6 J dissipated to thermal stores of the ball and the surrounding air.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think energy is used up or destroyed, for example when a battery goes flat.
misconceptions.right: In fact energy is never destroyed. It is transferred to other stores, usually ending up dissipated in the thermal stores of the surroundings.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often list heat, light, sound and electrical energy as types of energy store.
misconceptions.right: In fact heating, radiation (light and sound) and electrical work are pathways that transfer energy. The stores are kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an object at the top of its flight has no energy because it has stopped.
misconceptions.right: In fact its kinetic store is empty at that instant, but its gravitational potential store is at its maximum.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a closed system means a physically sealed container.
misconceptions.right: In fact a closed system is one where no energy enters or leaves, so the total energy is constant.

realWorld: Car engineers track how the chemical store of fuel is redistributed into kinetic stores and wasted thermal stores to design more economical vehicles.
Roller coaster designers use the exchange between gravitational potential and kinetic stores to plan the heights of hills so the cars have enough energy to complete the ride.
Food labels give the energy in the chemical store of food in kJ, which the body transfers to kinetic and thermal stores.
examTips: Always name the store AND say whether it increases or decreases, for example 'the kinetic store of the car decreases'.
Do not write 'heat energy' or 'movement energy'; use the AQA terms 'thermal store' and 'kinetic store'.
When asked how energy is transferred, name the pathway: mechanically (by a force doing work), electrically, by heating or by radiation.
In redistribution calculations, convert everything to the same unit (usually J) before adding or subtracting.
summary: A system is an object or group of objects.
There are eight energy stores and four transfer pathways.
Energy is conserved: it is transferred, stored or dissipated, never created or destroyed.
A closed system has no net change in total energy.
The decrease in one store equals the total increase in the others.
Wasted energy usually ends up in the thermal stores of the surroundings.

flashcards.back: An object or group of objects.

flashcards.back: Mechanically (work by a force), electrically, by heating, by radiation.

flashcards.front: Energy changes for a ball thrown upwards
flashcards.back: Kinetic store decreases, gravitational potential store increases.

flashcards.front: Energy changes when a car brakes
flashcards.back: Kinetic store decreases; thermal stores of the brakes and surroundings increase.

flashcards.front: Energy changes in an electric kettle
flashcards.back: Energy transferred electrically to the element, then by heating to the thermal store of the water.

flashcards.front: Which store does a stretched spring have?
Which store does a battery have?
What happens to energy that is wasted?
flashcards.back: It is dissipated, usually to the thermal stores of the surroundings.
No. It can be transferred, stored or dissipated but never created or destroyed.

questions.question: Which of these is an energy store?
options: Heating
Kinetic
Radiation
Electrical work
markScheme: 1 mark: Kinetic
questions.explanation: Kinetic is a store (energy of a moving object). Heating, radiation and electrical work are pathways that transfer energy between stores.

questions.question: A rubber band is stretched and held. In which store is energy now held?
options: Gravitational potential store
Thermal store
Elastic potential store
Chemical store
markScheme: 1 mark: Elastic potential store
questions.explanation: Stretched or squashed objects store energy in an elastic potential store. Gravitational potential needs a change of height, and the band has not been heated or reacted chemically.

questions.question: Which pathway transfers energy when an electric current flows through a motor?
options: Mechanically
Electrically
By heating
By radiation
markScheme: 1 mark: Electrically
questions.explanation: When charge flows (a current), work is done electrically. The motor then transfers energy mechanically, but the pathway into the motor is electrical.

questions.question: A battery-powered torch is switched on. Which energy store decreases?
options: The chemical store of the battery
The kinetic store of the torch
The nuclear store of the bulb
The elastic potential store of the battery
markScheme: 1 mark: The chemical store of the battery
questions.explanation: A battery stores energy chemically. When the torch is on, energy is transferred electrically from the battery's chemical store to the bulb, then by radiation and heating to the surroundings.

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Air resistance can be ignored. Which statement describes the energy change as the ball rises?
options: The gravitational potential store decreases and the kinetic store increases
Both the kinetic store and the gravitational potential store increase
The kinetic store decreases and energy is transferred to the chemical store
The kinetic store decreases and the gravitational potential store increases
markScheme: 1 mark: The kinetic store decreases and the gravitational potential store increases
questions.explanation: As the ball rises it slows down (kinetic store decreases) and gains height (gravitational potential store increases). The first option describes a falling ball. Both cannot increase because energy is conserved.

questions.question: A car brakes and comes to a stop. Which statement is correct?
options: The kinetic energy of the car is destroyed by the brakes
The kinetic store of the car is transferred back to the chemical store of the fuel
The kinetic store of the car decreases and the thermal stores of the brakes and surroundings increase
The thermal store of the brakes decreases
markScheme: 1 mark: The kinetic store of the car decreases and the thermal stores of the brakes and surroundings increase
questions.explanation: Friction in the brakes does work, transferring energy mechanically from the kinetic store to thermal stores, so the brakes get hot. Energy is never destroyed, and ordinary brakes cannot refill the fuel tank.

questions.question: What is meant by a closed system?
options: A system sealed so that no air can get in or out
A system where no energy is transferred in or out, so the total energy does not change
A system in which energy is gradually used up
A system that contains only one object
markScheme: 1 mark: A system where no energy is transferred in or out, so the total energy does not change
questions.explanation: In physics a closed system is defined by energy: no energy enters or leaves, so there is no net change in total energy. It need not be airtight, and a system can contain many objects.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the energy transfer when water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle?
options: Energy is transferred by radiation from the nuclear store of the kettle
The chemical store of the water increases
Energy is transferred mechanically to the kinetic store of the kettle
Energy is transferred electrically to the heating element, which then heats the water, increasing its thermal store
markScheme: 1 mark: Energy is transferred electrically to the heating element, which then heats the water, increasing its thermal store
questions.explanation: The mains supply does electrical work on the element. The hot element transfers energy by heating to the water, so the water's thermal store increases. No chemical or nuclear change happens.

questions.question: A trolley on a level, frictionless track is pulled by a constant horizontal force. Which statement describes the energy change?
options: Work done by the force increases the kinetic store of the trolley
The force increases the gravitational potential store of the trolley
The kinetic store stays constant because the force is constant
The force transfers energy to the thermal store of the track by friction
markScheme: 1 mark: Work done by the force increases the kinetic store of the trolley
questions.explanation: A constant resultant force accelerates the trolley, so its speed and kinetic store keep increasing. The track is level (no change in GPE) and frictionless (no heating of the track). A constant force does not mean constant speed.

questions.question: A ball is dropped onto a hard floor. Each bounce is lower than the one before. What is the best explanation?
options: Energy is destroyed every time the ball hits the floor
The gravitational field strength increases after each bounce
At each bounce some energy is dissipated to the thermal stores of the ball and floor and carried away as sound
The chemical store of the ball increases at each bounce
markScheme: 1 mark: At each bounce some energy is dissipated to the thermal stores of the ball and floor and carried away as sound
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved, but at each impact (and through air resistance) some energy is dissipated to thermal stores and as sound. Less energy remains to transfer back into the gravitational potential store, so the ball rises less high.

questions.question: A cyclist speeds up. Her chemical store decreases by 1.5 kJ and her kinetic store increases by 420 J. Calculate the energy dissipated to the surroundings. Give your answer in joules.
markScheme: 1 mark: 1.5 kJ = 1500 J
questions.explanation: Convert to joules first: 1.5 kJ = 1500 J. Energy is conserved, so dissipated energy = 1500 − 420 = 1080 J. Subtracting 420 from 1.5 gives a meaningless answer because the units differ.

questions.question: The chemical store of the battery in a toy car decreases by 450 J. The kinetic store of the car increases by 90 J and 60 J is transferred as sound. The rest is transferred to thermal stores. Calculate the energy transferred to thermal stores.
questions.explanation: Total energy is conserved: 450 J = 90 J + 60 J + thermal, so thermal = 450 − 150 = 300 J.

questions.question: As a car accelerates, the chemical store of its fuel decreases by 2400 kJ. The kinetic store of the car increases by 600 kJ. Assume all the remaining energy is dissipated to thermal stores. Calculate the energy dissipated in kJ.
questions.explanation: Both values are already in kJ, so subtract directly: 2400 − 600 = 1800 kJ is dissipated. Most of the fuel's energy in a car is wasted heating the engine and surroundings.

questions.question: A ball has 12 J in its gravitational potential store when it is dropped. Just before it hits the ground its kinetic store is 11.4 J. Calculate the energy transferred to the thermal stores of the ball and the air during the fall.
markScheme: 1 mark: recognises GPE lost = KE gained + energy dissipated
questions.explanation: All 12 J leaves the gravitational potential store. 11.4 J goes to the kinetic store, so 12 − 11.4 = 0.6 J was transferred by work done against air resistance to thermal stores.

questions.question: A spring launcher fires a ball straight up. The elastic potential store of the spring is 2.5 J. At its highest point the ball's gravitational potential store has increased by 2.1 J. Calculate the percentage of the initial energy that was dissipated.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy dissipated = 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4 J
questions.explanation: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic store is zero. Dissipated energy = 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4 J. As a percentage: 0.4 ÷ 2.5 × 100 = 16%. Giving 0.4 or 84% are common errors.

questions.question: State what is meant by a system in physics.
acceptedAnswers: an object or group of objects
markScheme: 1 mark: an object or group of objects
questions.explanation: AQA defines a system as an object or group of objects. We then track how energy is redistributed within it when it changes.

questions.question: Name the four ways in which energy can be transferred between stores.
markScheme: 2 marks: all four of mechanically (by a force doing work), electrically, by heating, by radiation
1 mark: two or three correct
questions.explanation: These are the energy pathways. Light and sound are examples of radiation. Do not confuse pathways with stores.

questions.question: A car is driven to the top of a hill. State which energy store of the car has increased because of its new position.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravitational potential (store)
questions.explanation: Raising an object in a gravitational field increases its gravitational potential store. Its speed may be the same, so the kinetic store need not change.

questions.question: A battery-powered fan is switched on. Describe the changes in the way energy is stored.
acceptedAnswers: chemical store of the battery decreases
kinetic store of the blades increases
markScheme: 1 mark: chemical store of the battery decreases
1 mark: energy transferred electrically to the motor
1 mark: kinetic store of the blades increases, with some energy dissipated to thermal stores of the surroundings (or as sound)
questions.explanation: The battery's chemical store falls; current carries energy electrically to the motor; the motor does work making the blades spin (kinetic store). Some energy is wasted heating the motor and as sound.

questions.question: Explain why the total energy of a closed system stays the same when the system changes.
acceptedAnswers: energy cannot be created or destroyed
energy is only transferred between stores
markScheme: 1 mark: no energy is transferred into or out of a closed system
1 mark: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores within the system
questions.explanation: By definition, nothing crosses the boundary of a closed system. Inside, conservation of energy means any decrease in one store is matched by increases in others.

questions.question: An apple falls from a tree. Air resistance can be ignored. Describe the energy transfer as the apple falls.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravitational potential store of the apple decreases
1 mark: kinetic store increases (energy transferred mechanically by the weight doing work)
questions.explanation: As the apple loses height its gravitational potential store decreases. The weight does work on it, so it speeds up and its kinetic store increases by the same amount.

questions.question: A cyclist free-wheels (does not pedal) down a hill at a constant speed. Explain what happens to the energy in the cyclist and bicycle's stores.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravitational potential store decreases
1 mark: kinetic store stays constant because speed is constant
1 mark: energy is transferred by work done against air resistance and friction to the thermal stores of the surroundings (dissipated)
questions.explanation: Constant speed means no change in the kinetic store. The decrease in gravitational potential store therefore all goes into work against resistive forces, ending up as thermal energy in the air, tyres and road.

questions.question: A student says 'when my phone battery goes flat, its energy has been used up'. Explain why this statement is wrong.
acceptedAnswers: energy cannot be created or destroyed
markScheme: 1 mark: energy cannot be created or destroyed (it is conserved)
1 mark: the energy from the chemical store has been transferred to other stores, mostly dissipated to the thermal stores of the surroundings
questions.explanation: The chemical store has decreased, but the same amount of energy now exists in other stores, mainly spread out as thermal energy in the surroundings where it is no longer useful.

questions.question: An electric kettle is used to bring some water to the boil. Describe the energy transfers that take place, including any energy that is wasted.
markScheme: Indicative content: energy is transferred electrically from the mains to the heating element; the element's thermal store increases; energy is transferred by heating from the element to the water; the thermal store of the water increases and its temperature rises; some energy is transferred by heating to the kettle body and the surroundings; some is carried away by sound; this wasted energy is dissipated.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear, logical description naming the pathways and stores, including at least one wasted transfer.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct stores or pathways named but the sequence is unclear or incomplete.
questions.explanation: A good answer follows the energy in order: electrically to the element, by heating to the water's thermal store, with some dissipated to the kettle and air and as sound.

questions.question:
A tennis ball is thrown vertically upwards. It reaches its maximum height, falls back down, hits the ground and bounces.
Describe the changes in the way energy is stored during this whole process. Include the effect of air resistance.
markScheme: Indicative content: just after release the kinetic store is at its maximum; as the ball rises its kinetic store decreases and its gravitational potential store increases; at maximum height the kinetic store is zero and the gravitational potential store is at its maximum; as it falls the gravitational potential store decreases and the kinetic store increases; air resistance does work against the ball throughout, transferring energy to the thermal stores of the ball and air; on impact the ball squashes so the kinetic store transfers to the elastic potential store, which then transfers back to the kinetic store as it bounces; some energy is dissipated as sound and to thermal stores at impact; so the ball does not return to its original height; total energy is conserved.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, coherent description covering rising, falling and bouncing, correctly using store names, and explaining that air resistance and the bounce dissipate energy so the bounce height is lower, with reference to conservation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct description of the kinetic and gravitational potential changes with some mention of energy being dissipated.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about kinetic or gravitational potential stores changing.
questions.explanation: Track each stage separately: rising (KE to GPE), top (GPE maximum), falling (GPE to KE), impact (KE to elastic potential and back). At every stage some energy is dissipated, which explains the lower bounce.

questions.question:
A car travelling along a level road brakes to stop at traffic lights, then accelerates away again.
Describe the changes in energy stores for the car while it stops and while it accelerates.
markScheme: Indicative content: while braking the kinetic store of the car decreases; friction between the brake pads and discs does work; the thermal stores of the brakes increase and energy is dissipated to the surroundings; while accelerating the chemical store of the fuel (or battery) decreases; the engine does work and the kinetic store of the car increases; some energy is dissipated to thermal stores of the engine and surroundings and as sound.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both stages described with correct stores and pathways and mention of dissipation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one stage described correctly, or simple statements about kinetic energy changing.
questions.explanation: Braking converts kinetic store to thermal stores through friction. Accelerating takes energy from the chemical store of the fuel to the kinetic store, with large losses to thermal stores.

questions.question: Name the energy store that decreases as a hot cup of tea cools down.
markScheme: 1 mark: thermal (internal) store
questions.explanation: A hot object has a large thermal store. As the tea cools it transfers energy by heating to the surroundings, so its thermal store decreases.

questions.question: Two magnets are pushed together so that their north poles are close and they repel. They are held in place. Which store has increased?
options: Magnetic store
Kinetic store
Nuclear store
Chemical store
markScheme: 1 mark: Magnetic store
questions.explanation: Work is done pushing repelling magnets together, and this energy is held in the magnetic store. They are held still, so the kinetic store has not increased.
